title: Their angels (Matthew 18:1–14)
hookLine: who's the greatest? a child in the middle, and angels before God's face
tomorrow: someone hurt you. where does Jesus say to start?

lines: NOT WHO'S TOP: WHO GETS IN.
cards: Greatest of all time: the internet runs that argument every week, about athletes, albums, pizza. The disciples run their version: "Who is the greatest in the kingdom of heaven?" Here's yesterday's question answered.

Jesus calls a little child, sets him in the middle of them, and answers with the child. "Except ye be converted, and become as little children, ye shall not enter into the kingdom of heaven." They asked who's at the top.

teach.b: Then the line this day is named for: "Take heed that ye despise not one of these little ones; for I say unto you, That in heaven their angels do always behold the face of my Father which is in heaven." Their angels.
Christians read those two words in more than one way, and both readings have a real case.

teach.h: GUARDIAN ANGELS: TAKE IT AS SAID.
teach.b: Catholics and Orthodox Christians speak of guardian angels, and the Catholic Catechism points to this verse: Jesus says the little ones have angels of their own, and he says it plainly, in the present tense.
Why explain it away? Some Protestant readers hold the verse more lightly.

Angels are real to them too, but they hear this as a picture of nearness: the people nobody notices are the ones closest to God's face. Build a whole teaching on one verse, they say, and you may say more than Jesus did.
Notice where both sides end up, though. Neither lets anyone look down on a child.
And Jesus goes straight on to a shepherd with a hundred sheep who leaves the ninety and nine to find one that wandered.
"Even so it is not the will of your Father which is in heaven, that one of these little ones should perish."

how: Catholic and Orthodox Christians speak of guardian angels and some teach children a short prayer to their angel; other Christians read Matthew 18:10 as a picture of God's closeness to the small.

o: the spirits of children who have died
the twelve disciples, called God's messengers
the little ones' angels, who see God's face

games.q: who's in Matthew 18 — tap the pairs.
p: set in the middle of them

s: Matthew 18 says children become angels when they die
the verse speaks of their angels in heaven beholding God's face. it doesn't say children become angels.
the Catholic Catechism points to this verse when it speaks of guardian angels
and some Protestant readers hear the same words as a picture of God's nearness to the small.
Jesus answers 'who is the greatest?' by naming one of the disciples
he sets a little child in the middle and talks about who gets in at all.

games.q: your friend says 'their angels' is just a picture of God's nearness, nothing more. state the other side's best case.
o: Jesus says plainly that the little ones have angels of their own, before God.
the verse names each child's angel and lists what it does all day.
every church has always taught it the same way, so it settles it.
games.why: the guardian-angel reading rests on the words themselves: their angels, in heaven, always beholding God's face. the other side reads the same words as nearness. both refuse to despise a little one.

practice: Find a photo of yourself as a small child, or bring one to mind: the haircut, the shoes, the expression. Look at that face for the length of the sit, without grading it.
Then let your eyes rest on one child you know now, in a photo or in memory, and look at them the same way.

wordCard.voice: Their angels. Jesus' words for the little ones' angels, who always behold the Father's face.

orig.note: Greek: a little child, the word for the child Jesus sets in the middle in Matthew 18:2.

carryVoice: Something to keep: their angels see God, and nobody is too small to be watched over. Day done.
